items.a: Consultify is an AI-powered strategic consulting platform that helps industrial organizations navigate digital transformation. It combines artificial intelligence with human governance to deliver actionable roadmaps, not just reports.

items.q: How is this different from traditional consulting?
items.a: Traditional consulting delivers PowerPoint decks. Consultify delivers a living system. Our AI continuously analyzes your context, generates initiatives, and tracks execution. You get real-time strategic guidance, not a one-time report that sits on a shelf.

Absolutely. We are GDPR compliant with EU data residency. All data is encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3). We never train AI models on your proprietary data. Enterprise customers can use their own API keys (BYOK).

items.q: Do I need technical expertise to use it?
items.a: No. Consultify is designed for business leaders, not IT specialists. The interface is intuitive, and our AI guides you through every step. We also offer onboarding support and training for your team.

items.q: Can I try before I buy?
items.a: Yes! We offer a 7-day free trial with full access to all features. No credit card required. You can also request a personalized demo with our team to see the platform in action with your specific use case.

We specialize in manufacturing and industrial sectors, including automotive, aerospace, electronics, food & beverage, and heavy industry. Our assessment frameworks are tailored to Industry 4.0 transformation challenges.

0.question: How do I earn commissions as a partner?
0.answer: You earn commissions by referring new clients to Consultify. When a client signs up using your unique referral code or link and becomes a paying customer, you receive a percentage of their subscription fee. Discount rates range from 10% to 14% depending on your partner tier.

1.question: When and how do I get paid?
1.answer: Commissions are paid monthly via bank transfer or PayPal, once you reach the €100 minimum threshold. Payments are processed on the 15th of each month for the previous month's approved commissions. You can track all earnings in real-time through your Partner Dashboard.

2.question: What support do I get as a partner?
2.answer: All partners receive access to Partner Academy training, marketing materials, and our partner community. Bronze tier and above get priority support and dedicated training. Gold and Platinum partners receive a dedicated Partner Manager, co-marketing opportunities, and early access to new features.

3.question: How long does it take to become certified?
3.answer: The Platform Fundamentals certification takes about 45 minutes to complete. Advanced certifications like DRD Framework take 2-3 hours. All certifications are self-paced, so you can complete them whenever it's convenient for you.

4.question: Can I refer clients from any country?
4.answer: Yes! Consultify operates globally, and you can refer clients from any country. Your Partner Directory listing can highlight your regional expertise, helping local clients find you. Commission payments can be made in EUR, USD, or GBP.

5.question: What happens if a referred client cancels?
5.answer: If a referred client cancels within the first 30 days (cooling-off period), the commission for that client is adjusted. After 30 days, you keep all earned commissions even if the client later cancels. We believe in fair, transparent commission structures.

insightCreatorModal.analyzeRespondentAnswersAtA:
Analyze respondent answers at a deep level. Look for:
1. HIDDEN INTENTIONS — what the respondent really wants to achieve but doesn't say directly
2. CONTRADICTIONS — where one person's answers are inconsistent or contradict others
3. EVASIONS — topics respondents avoid or downplay
4. UNSPOKEN GOALS — political goals, personal interests, hidden agendas
5. EMOTIONS & TENSIONS — where you see frustration, fear, enthusiasm, or resistance
6. LIES & EXAGGERATION — answers that seem implausible or exaggerated

For each finding provide: quote, interpretation, confidence level (high/medium/low), and recommendation.
insightCreatorModal.useAPreciseConsultingFormula:
Use a precise consulting formula:
1. CONTEXT (2-3 sentences) — interview purpose, scope, number of respondents
2. KEY FINDINGS (5-7 points) — most important discoveries, ranked by impact
3. PATTERNS & TRENDS — recurring themes, common concerns
4. DIVERGENCES — where opinions differ and why
5. RISKS & OPPORTUNITIES — identified threats and possibilities (facts-only; no recommendations or next steps)

styles.friendlyDesc: Warm, casual tone, like chatting with a good friend

stylePresets.concise: Respond briefly and directly, using as few words as possible. Focus on the core point without elaboration or follow-up questions.
stylePresets.executive: Respond like a senior consulting partner. Start with the recommendation, then 3-5 bullets with rationale. Add risks and next steps. Skip introductions.
stylePresets.analyst: Respond like a data analyst. Use tables, metrics, and benchmarks. Cite sources and confidence intervals. Structure data for easy further analysis.
stylePresets.formal: Use a formal, professional tone. Write clear, well-structured sentences with precise language. Maintain professionalism and avoid colloquialisms. Provide thorough explanations while remaining concise, as if addressing a board-level colleague.
stylePresets.coach: Respond as a coach and mentor. Instead of giving direct answers, ask guiding questions. Walk through reasoning step by step, helping discover insights independently.
stylePresets.professional: Respond like an experienced strategy consultant. Use the structure: situation → analysis → recommendation → next steps. Provide specific metrics and KPIs. Reference frameworks (SWOT, Porter, BCG matrix). Use precise business language with a clear action plan.
stylePresets.friendly: Respond warmly and casually, like a good friend. Use simple language, add emoji where they fit. Be supportive, enthusiastic, and positive. Keep it approachable but still helpful and on-point.

menu.customInstructionsPlaceholder: e.g. "Always respond in English", "I prefer tables over text", "I am a CTO at a manufacturing company"
menu.customInstructionsDesc: These preferences are applied to every response in Chat.
menu.customInstructionsStarter1: I prefer short, actionable answers with a checklist and clear owners.
menu.customInstructionsStarter2: Use tables when comparing options. Always include risks and mitigations.
menu.customInstructionsStarter3: Ask 2-3 clarifying questions when the request is ambiguous before answering.
menu.customInstructionsStarter4: Write in Polish and keep a professional consulting tone.
menu.customInstructionsTip: Tip: mention your role, industry, and preferred output format.

ai.anomalyCopy: Automatic detection of outliers in the KPI measurement series — via z-score (|z| > 2) and IQR (outside Q1−1.5·IQR / Q3+1.5·IQR). A point flagged by both methods or at |z| ≥ 3 is marked severe.
ai.anomalyServerNote: Anomalies are computed server-side (kpiAnomalyService engine) — results appear here once the KPI measurement endpoint is wired.
ai.forecastCopy: Linear regression (least squares) on each KPI's measurement history: value forecast, estimated time to target (ETA) and a leading alert when the trend misses target before the deadline.
ai.forecastConfidence: Confidence: low / medium / high (from measurement count + R² fit)
ai.forecastMinPoints: Requires min. 6 measurements per KPI. kpiForecastService engine — available after AI premium configuration.
ai.rcaCopy: For each KPI deviation a heuristic engine (no LLM, deterministic) generates root-cause hypotheses from signals: deviation, trend, adoption, data freshness, scope change, resource overload — and maps them to concrete corrective actions with an owner.
ai.rcaServerNote: Suggestions are computed server-side (deviationRcaSuggestService engine) — they appear here for detected deviations once the RCA endpoint is wired.

## Decision Context

This decision concerns selecting the optimal solution for {{title}}.

### Background
The analysis has identified the following key factors:
- Business and technical requirements
- Budget and timeline constraints
- Impact on existing processes

### Scope
The decision covers:
1. Vendor/technology selection
2. Implementation timeline definition
3. Resource allocation

### Expected Outcomes
- Process efficiency improvement
- Operational cost reduction
- Increased competitiveness

seed.understanding: I understand this session as an attempt to define the strategic direction for the whole organization, not just improve a single KPI. Dynamic SWOT should help name where the company should go, what advantage it can build on, and which choices matter most for leadership now.
seed.goal: How should the company define its next strategic direction so that growth, market position, and execution capability reinforce one another?
seed.scope: The analysis covers the whole company: offer, customer segments, growth model, core operating capabilities, organizational constraints, and market factors that shape the strategic choice.
seed.successSignal: By the end of the session, leadership should have an agreed strategic direction, a clear logic of choice, the top priorities, and a set of moves that can be translated into decisions and execution.
seed.kpiTarget: 12-18 months for directional change, 90 days for the first moves and execution decisions
seed.constraints: The direction must be realistic for current resources; we do not assume a full transformation of everything at once; the recommendation must be clear for leadership and translatable into next decisions.
seed.assumptions: The company has several possible growth paths, but no shared answer yet on which one truly builds advantage; some tensions come from the market, others from inside the organization; leadership needs material that structures the choice instead of merely describing the situation.

summary.intro: This Dynamic SWOT is meant to build decision material for leadership, not just a neat diagnosis. Its role is to identify the strategic direction the organization should consider most sensible, and show why that choice deserves to be carried forward into actions, priorities, and subsequent decisions.
summary.body: Based on the answers so far, this session should focus on: {{direction}}. At the center of the analysis should sit: {{scope}}. That means the SWOT should not merely describe the situation, but structure the strategic choice, surface the tensions, name the constraints, and show which decision logic is most justified today.
summary.delivery: The intended delivery of this work is an outcome shaped as: {{success}}. To make that outcome credible, the session must additionally answer: {{question4}}, while respecting the boundaries: {{question5}}. This is the exact fragment that should later become the first slide of the presentation, explaining the purpose of the SWOT, the scope of work, and the intended logic of delivery.

riskUncertaintyLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Risk & Uncertainty moves from signals to safeguards
riskUncertaintyLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from uncertainty to resilience moves
riskUncertaintyLibraryGraphic.subtitle: The tool does not produce a fear list. It captures signals, builds assumptions, risks, and scenarios, requires card approval, and only then recommends validation, mitigation, monitoring, and escalation.
riskUncertaintyLibraryGraphic.missionProcess: Risk mission, scope, success signal, and constraints
riskUncertaintyLibraryGraphic.missionExample: How do we protect a transformation from delays, cost pressure, and demand shifts?
cards: What must be true for the strategy to work
What can hit outcome, cost, timing, or reputation
How different futures change the decision

portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Portfolio Priority moves from evidence to decisions
portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from initiative list to resource allocation
portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.subtitle: BCG is not a decorative matrix. The tool captures signals, proposes portfolio cards, asks for user approval, and only then builds trade-offs, moves, and initiatives.
portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.missionProcess: Portfolio mission, scope, constraints, and success signal
portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.missionExample: Which products and initiatives should receive funding next quarter under a constrained budget?
quadrants: High growth and strong position: invest selectively
High growth and weak position: test or choose the bet
Stable position: maintain and fund growth
Weak position: reduce, harvest, or redesign
portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.insight: The recommendation is not equal support for every topic, but deliberate allocation: invest, maintain, test, harvest, stop.
portfolioPriorityLibraryGraphic.output: Source summary -> portfolio initiatives -> deck -> report

growthPathsLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Growth Paths moves from ambition to path selection
growthPathsLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from growth ambition to a move sequence
growthPathsLibraryGraphic.subtitle: Ansoff is not an idea list. It frames ambition and evidence first, builds options across four fields, compares trade-offs, and only then moves into actions and initiatives.
growthPathsLibraryGraphic.missionProcess: Growth mission, scope, success signal, and constraints
growthPathsLibraryGraphic.missionExample: How do we grow premium-segment revenue without diluting margin?
quadrants: Use the current segment and channels better
New value propositions for current customers
New product and new market, highest risk
growthPathsLibraryGraphic.insight: The recommendation does not come from the longest idea list, but from the best sequence: scale core, test the new segment, then increase risk.

marketForcesLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Market Forces moves from market structure to decision
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from market pressure to a move sequence
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.subtitleProcess: This is not a static Five Forces checklist. First we frame the market and decision, then collect evidence, score competitive pressure, and translate it into moves and initiatives.
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.subtitleExample: This case shows that a strong Porter session does not stop at a scorecard. It captures signals first, scores the forces next, and only then builds implications, moves, and outputs.
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueProcess: The session starts with industry, geography, company position, and the decision question. Without that, the force scorecard becomes abstract.
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueExample: Ateliertoy is considering entering a B2B marketplace segment. The real question is whether the market offers a defensible position or whether platform and buyer pressure will consume margin faster than growth rebuilds it.
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.decisionValueProcess: A market attractiveness read, margin pressure logic, strategic levers, and outputs ready for downstream work.
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.decisionValueExample: Enter the marketplace now, or first build a partner channel and data advantage?
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.stage3Value: Score, trend, drivers, evidence, and confidence
marketForcesLibraryGraphic.stage5Value: Moves, initiatives, report, deck, or idea
forces: High price pressure and easily copied offers
Entry is possible, but requires channel and trust
Alternatives exist but do not solve the full job
Large customers force discounts and SLA terms
Input costs move, but can be diversified
implicationItems: The market may grow, but advantage without data and channel will be fragile.
The biggest risk sits in buyer power and offer comparability.
moveItems: Build partner channel and demand data first.
Treat marketplace entry as a step after margin validation.
Close the result as an initiative brief and board deck.

narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Narrative Engine builds a message house around one idea
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from one core message to a message house with pillars
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.subtitleProcess: This is not a loose set of messages. First we frame the audience and core message (the roof), then 3-4 pillars (columns), each with its own claim and proof, with color showing audience resonance.
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.subtitleExample: This case shows that a narrative is not a pile of slides. It sets one core message first (the roof), then the pillars (columns) that hold it up, and the proof points each pillar carries.
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueProcess: The session starts with the audience, goal, and core message. Without a roof the pillars have nothing to hold, and proof points are detached from the decision.
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueExample: The board hears ten arguments at once and none of them sticks. The real question is which single idea they should remember and which three pillars actually hold it up.
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.decisionValueProcess: One core message as the roof, 3-4 pillars with a claim and proof points, tagged by audience resonance, ready for narrative, report, and deck.
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.decisionValueExample: Which single idea should stick, and which pillars with proof points hold it up?
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.coreValue: Without AI we lose the market in 18 months
narrativeEngineLibraryGraphic.footer: Narrative Engine = brief -> core message -> pillars -> proof -> narrative -> outputs

capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Capability Mapper moves from maturity to priorities
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from capability maturity to build/buy/partner moves
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.subtitleProcess: This is not a static competency inventory. First we frame strategy and domains, score current vs target maturity on a 1-5 scale, weight by strategic importance, and translate gaps into moves and initiatives.
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.subtitleExample: This case shows that a capability map is not a competency checklist. It scores current and target maturity first, weighs strategic importance, and only then surfaces gaps and moves.
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueProcess: The session starts with industry, capability domains, strategic priorities, and the decision question. Without that, maturity scoring is detached from strategy.
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueExample: A company wants to move into AI but does not know which capabilities it truly lacks. The real question is where the gap between current and target is widest exactly where strategic importance is highest.
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.decisionValueProcess: Each capability's current vs target maturity, prioritized gaps, and build/buy/partner moves ready for downstream work.
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.decisionValueExample: Which capabilities must be raised first for the strategy to move at all?
capabilityMapperLibraryGraphic.footer: Capability Mapper = brief -> capabilities -> maturity -> gaps -> moves -> outputs

focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Focus & Trade-offs moves from value and effort to decisions
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.titleExample: Example: from competing priorities to pursue/defer/drop moves
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.subtitleProcess: This is not a wishlist sorted by gut feel. First we frame competing priorities and decision criteria, score value vs effort on a 1-5 scale, map them onto a matrix, and translate positions into pursue/defer/drop moves.
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.subtitleExample: This case shows that prioritization is not a wishlist ranking. It weighs the value and effort of each option first, maps them onto a matrix, and only then recommends what to pursue, defer, or drop.
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueProcess: The session starts with competing priorities, decision criteria, the goal, and constraints. Without that, value and effort scoring is detached from strategy.
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.scenarioValueExample: A team has more initiatives than capacity and everyone defends their own. The real question is which deliver the most value for the least effort and which only drain the team.
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.decisionValueProcess: Each priority's value vs effort score, its position on the 2x2 matrix, and pursue/defer/drop moves ready for downstream work.
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.decisionValueExample: Which priorities do we pursue now, and which do we deliberately defer or drop?
stages: Quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pit
focusTradeoffLibraryGraphic.footer: Focus & Trade-offs = brief -> priorities -> value vs effort -> matrix -> moves -> outputs

ambitionDecomposerLibraryGraphic.titleProcess: How Ambition Decomposer breaks an ambition into measurable themes

goal.positioningHeadline: Dynamic SWOT is not meant to fill a matrix. It is meant to turn a fragmented strategic conversation into a decision, tensions, and moves ready for downstream use.
goal.positioningBody: This is a conversation-first, structure-backed tool. It frames the strategic question and structures evidence from inside the company and the market first. Only then does it build the matrix, surface tensions, sequence recommended moves, and prepare material that can feed a report, presentation, initiatives, or further decision work.
whatItDoes: separates the critical signals from noise, opinion, and generic statements
builds one shared picture of internal and external reality
turns classic SWOT into tension, trade-off, and decision logic
takes the user from diagnosis to a recommended move and downstream outputs
whatItIsNot: it is not a classroom exercise about filling four boxes
it is not a dump for everything without assessing evidence quality
it is not a way to fake a decision when the strategic question is still vague
it is not the final deliverable, but the source for deliverables and execution
whenToUse: when leadership has many signals but no single decision logic
when internal reality must be confronted with the market and translated into what truly changes the direction
when the decision matters but the situation still looks like disconnected observations
when the result must feed a report, deck, initiative, or decision brief
whenNotToUse: when the first job is to understand macro trends, context, or regulation: start with PESTEL
when the core question is industry structure and competitive pressure: start with Five Forces
when the decision has already been made and only execution planning is needed: use initiative planning instead
when the team wants only positive mobilization language without working through risk and weakness
prepare: a concrete strategic question that truly needs a decision
scope, time horizon, success signal, and the key constraints
known internal and external signals, even if still incomplete
files, links, benchmarks, interview notes, or prior analyses
goal.dynamicLabel: What makes the SWOT dynamic here
goal.dynamicBody: The classical matrix is only the middle step. The dynamic version forces stronger framing first, then signal and evidence hygiene, and only then moves into TOWS-style connection logic, tensions, and strategic moves.

process.intro: A strong Dynamic SWOT runs through five business steps. The flow is simple for the user but rigorous in substance: frame the decision first, clean the signals second, build a strong matrix third, and only then move into tensions, moves, and outputs.

steps.oneLiner: Frame the decision question, scope, and success signal
items: name the decision that truly needs to be made
set the scope, time horizon, success signal, and constraints
separate the session topic from everything that is out of scope today
steps.note: The quality of the full session depends on the opening question. If the brief is vague, the matrix becomes only well-organized chaos.

steps.oneLiner: Collect facts, observations, and hypotheses from inside and outside
items: collect signals from interviews, materials, files, links, and benchmarks
mark whether an entry is a fact, observation, or hypothesis
separate internal from external signals and reduce each to one clear thesis
steps.note: This is not the stage for conclusions yet. It builds the source layer from which the later conclusions can be defended.

steps.oneLiner: Assign signals to S/W/O/T, remove noise, keep what moves the decision
items: assign the signals to Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats
remove duplicates, separate symptoms from causes, and challenge generic wording
keep only the cards that truly change the decision space
steps.note: A strong matrix is not long. It is selective, concrete, and backed by sources.

steps.oneLiner: Show where advantage collides with constraint or risk
items: connect cards into decision situations: attack, repair, defend, reduce
show where advantage meets constraint or risk
name why this tension matters now rather than later
steps.note: This is where consulting value appears. The card list stops being a table and starts becoming decision logic.

steps.oneLiner: Translate tensions into recommended moves and downstream material
items: translate the tensions into 2-4 recommended moves with a clear sequence
separate a quick win from a strategic move and from an item that still needs validation
close the session with a source summary ready for a report, deck, initiative, or further exploration
steps.note: Dynamic SWOT is only strong when it ends in a decision, a move, or a credible bridge to action.

process.sessionQualityLabel: What a strong finished session looks like
sessionQualityItems: a matrix with 6-12 selected factors across the 4 quadrants (S/W/O/T) — each with a marked source and evidence type, instead of a long list of everything
3-6 strategic tensions that genuinely explain the decision space
2-4 recommended moves with a clear sequence and first step
at least 1 output candidate ready for further decision or sponsor approval
a final source summary that can directly feed a report or deck
process.decisionSituationsIntro: In step 4 you connect internal factors with external ones. Each connection creates one of four decision situations. Recognizing the type helps quickly decide what move makes sense.

decisionSituationsCards.label: Strength + Opportunity
decisionSituationsCards.desc: You have advantage and the market offers an opening. Play offensively — use what you have to capture the opportunity.

decisionSituationsCards.label: Weakness + Opportunity
decisionSituationsCards.desc: The opportunity exists, but an internal gap blocks it. Fix the gap first, then move in.

decisionSituationsCards.label: Strength + Threat
decisionSituationsCards.desc: External risk is rising, but you have advantage. Use it to defend your position.

decisionSituationsCards.label: Weakness + Threat
decisionSituationsCards.desc: A weakness increases exposure to risk. Reduce the weakness first to lower the threat.

workingNotesItems: SWOT is not the goal, but a synthesis step on the way to a decision
the most common mistake is too many weak cards and too little selection
the quality of conclusions never exceeds the quality of source signals
a strong facilitator separates fact from hypothesis and symptom from cause
a strong session connects internal reality with the market instead of describing only one side
the output should be ready for management use, not only for the analyst to read

outcomes.intro: A strong Dynamic SWOT ends with usable material: the decision question, evidence quality, key tensions, and a move sequence.

blocks.title: Decision frame
blocks.what: The strategic question, scope, time horizon, and success signal. An explicit statement of what the analysis covers and what it does not.
blocks.why: Without this frame even a strong matrix drifts away from the real decision.
blocks.next: An executive summary with a clear decision frame for the sponsor or board.

blocks.title: Factor picture & evidence
blocks.what: The strongest S/W/O/T cards with their sources. A clear separation of facts, observations, and hypotheses.
blocks.why: Decision-makers see not only the conclusion, but the quality of the material underneath it.
blocks.next: A defensible matrix and narrative for the next decision discussion.

blocks.title: Strategic tensions
blocks.what: The most important connections between internal and external cards. Decision situations that change the move logic.
blocks.why: Observations stop being a list and start explaining where the real trade-off sits.
blocks.next: An interpretation layer for leadership discussion and priority choices.

blocks.title: Recommended moves
blocks.what: 2-4 moves emerging from tensions with a clear sequence. Quick win vs big bet vs defensive move vs capability build.
blocks.why: The handoff from diagnosis to a move that makes business sense and can be defended logically.
blocks.next: A shortlist of moves for the deck, sponsor decision, or initiative design.

blocks.title: Bridge to execution
blocks.what: A source summary ready for the report or presentation. What goes to an initiative, what needs a deck, what stays an idea.
blocks.why: SWOT without this step leaves the team with an interesting analysis but no move.
blocks.next: A report, presentation, initiative push, or further exploration from the same source package.

outcomes.qualityBody: A strong result is selective, evidence-backed, and decision-oriented. It does not show everything that was collected, only what truly changes the choice logic and enables the next step.

example.intro: This example shows a common transformation moment: pressure rises and technology looks like the quick answer, but the first job is to establish whether the real problem is the missing solution or the missing truth about the situation.

cases.title: Premium manufacturer before CAPEX
cases.context: Margin is falling, lead times are unstable, and leadership is considering automation.
cases.question: Should the company start with technology investment or diagnose losses and bottlenecks first?
evidence: Interviews show strong brand trust and premium customer relationships, but operational decisions are still intuition-led.
Data points to flow losses, no shared bottleneck definition, and rising expediting costs.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes SWOT cards around reputation and B2B trust, weak process visibility, a data-diagnosis opportunity, and the threat of automating the wrong problem.
cases.approvedUse: The user accepts only evidence-backed cards and rejects generic “implement AI” recommendations. Approved cards feed tensions and moves.
cases.outcome: The decision becomes: run loss diagnosis, bottleneck mapping, and a data layer before CAPEX, with automation as the second stage.

cases.title: Software firm after losing a major client
cases.context: The team is strong, but the sales pipeline depends too heavily on referrals.
cases.question: Should it scale outbound sales or first sharpen offer positioning?
evidence: CRM data shows long sales cycles outside referrals, while customer interviews reveal unclear offer differentiation.
The team has strong technical capability, but sales materials do not show measurable customer outcomes.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes SWOT cards on expert delivery, weak value narrative, an opportunity to verticalize the offer, and the threat of continued key-account dependency.
cases.approvedUse: Approved cards create the tension between delivery quality and weak ICP clarity, then shape moves before outbound scale.
cases.outcome: The sequence is: narrow ICP, build a customer proof pack, test two segment campaigns, and only then expand sales effort.

cases.title: Local services network before expansion
cases.context: Demand is growing, but operating quality varies across locations.
cases.question: Should the company open more sites or standardize the operating model first?
evidence: Customer reviews are excellent in the best locations, but complaints cluster around repeatable service steps.
Local managers interpret quality standards differently, and onboarding new staff takes too long.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes strengths in local brand and customer trust, weaknesses in operating standard, an expansion-playbook opportunity, and the threat of quality loss while scaling.
cases.approvedUse: Approved cards help decide whether the advantage is truly scalable or dependent on individual people and local habits.
cases.outcome: The recommendation is to build a service standard, quality dashboard, and training model before opening more sites.

situationItems: Ateliertoy is a premium company with in-house production and a strong B2B reputation
margin is under pressure, lead times are unstable, and leadership is considering expensive automation
the session question is whether the transformation should start with CAPEX or first with a diagnosis of losses, bottlenecks, and data blind spots
signalsItems: a strong brand and trusted premium customers are real advantages
operating decisions are still intuition-driven and there is no shared truth about losses and bottlenecks
the market increasingly expects faster delivery and higher predictability
there is a real risk of burning investment if automation starts before process diagnosis
matrixItems: Strengths: brand, B2B trust, in-house production, IP control
Weaknesses: no shared diagnosis, analog management, weak visibility into losses
Opportunities: digital diagnosis, stronger data layer, better sequencing of investments
Threats: price pressure, rising costs, and the risk of automating the wrong problem
tensionItems: the company has real assets to scale, but still lacks truth about where value is leaking today
automation looks attractive, yet without diagnosis it may only accelerate chaos
the main conclusion is to first see what truly constrains margin and flow, and only then choose the technology response
movesItems: run a diagnosis of losses, bottlenecks, and data blind spots before CAPEX
build one shared view of the process and the transformation priorities for leadership
only then sequence the roadmap: data -> automation -> investment governance
outputsItems: board-ready material explaining why the transformation should begin with diagnosis instead of a technology purchase
a short list of priorities and risks for the next transformation decisions
a source package for the roadmap, deck, and initiative generation in the platform
example.closingNote: This is a strong case because it does not stop at describing four quadrants. It shows how signals turn into a decision about move sequence and into material that can immediately bridge into execution.

goal.positioningHeadline: Market Forces is not a mechanical Five Forces scorecard. It turns market structure into a decision: where margin is pressured, where defensibility exists, and what move makes sense.
goal.positioningBody: This is an evidence-first, AI-assisted tool. It frames the industry, scope, company position, and decision question first. AI then helps capture signals from interviews and organization context, proposes the force scorecard, asks for user approval, and only then builds implications, moves, and initiatives from the approved diagnosis.
whatItDoes: connects organization and interview context with market signals
turns signals into a Five Forces scorecard with drivers, evidence, and confidence
shows margin pressure, buyer power, entry barriers, and defensibility
moves from market diagnosis into recommended moves and initiatives
whatItIsNot: it is not a dry Porter checklist without decision context
it is not a place to score a market without sources and signals
it does not auto-generate strategy without user approval
it does not stop at a radar or scorecard, but bridges into outputs
goal.aiPhilosophyBody: AI acts as an assisting consultant, not the source of truth. It proposes signals, force scores, implications, moves, and outputs, while the user accepts, rejects, or asks to rethink cards before they become initiative material.

process.intro: Market Forces runs through five phases analogous to Dynamic SWOT: mission, input, forces, insights, and outputs. Each phase has a different decision level and a different AI job.

steps.title: Mission & Market Context
steps.text: Industry, geography, position, question, and success signal

steps.title: Input & Exploration
steps.text: Signals from interviews, benchmarks, files, and observations

steps.title: Five Forces Build
steps.text: Each force scored with trend, drivers, evidence, and confidence

steps.title: Strategic Implications
steps.text: Margin pressure, defensibility, market tensions, and recommendations

steps.title: Outputs & Actions
steps.text: Source summary, output candidates, and initiative drafts

outcomes.intro: A strong outcome is decision-ready: it shows not only force scores, but also consequences for position, margin, and move sequence.

blocks.title: Five Forces scorecard
blocks.text: Scores, trends, drivers, evidence, and confidence for each force.

blocks.title: Strategic implications
blocks.text: What market structure means for margin, defensibility, and company position.

blocks.title: Recommended moves
blocks.text: 2-4 moves with rationale, effort, risk, and first step.

blocks.title: Output candidates

example.intro: A premium company is considering entering a new marketplace channel. Market Forces checks whether growth attractiveness will be consumed by buyer power, platform pressure, and easy offer imitation.

cases.title: Marketplace entry for a premium brand
cases.context: The company considers a high-reach channel with low control over customer relationship.
cases.question: Will volume growth be eaten by platform power and price pressure?
evidence: Interviews show customers like the brand, but marketplace buying is driven by price and delivery comparison.
Channel data shows high commissions, promotion cost, and easy imitation of best-selling items.
cases.aiDraft: AI scores buyer and platform power high, new entrants medium, and substitutes high in cheaper segments.
cases.approvedUse: The user approves evidence-backed drivers, and AI turns them into margin implications and defensible-entry conditions.
cases.outcome: The decision becomes a controlled pilot with limited SKU, price discipline, and a unique bundle that is hard to compare directly.

cases.title: New B2B segment for a services firm
cases.context: The company wants larger clients with longer and more formal buying processes.
cases.question: Does market attractiveness offset buyer power and sales cost?
evidence: Sales interviews show larger contracts, but stronger procurement, longer RFPs, and higher reference requirements.
Competitive benchmarks show segment leaders with certifications, case studies, and heavier pre-sales.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes high buyer power, high reputation barriers, and moderate rivalry in specialized niches.
cases.approvedUse: Approved cards identify which entry barriers must be built before broad sales scaling.
cases.outcome: The recommendation is to start with a B2B niche, build references and proof assets, then expand into enterprise.

cases.title: Manufacturer before international entry
cases.context: The market is large, but local players own distribution and channel relationships.
cases.question: Can entry work without a partner or a distinct cost advantage?
evidence: Market data shows strong demand, but a few distributors dominate access and shelf acquisition is expensive.
Interviews suggest local customers trust current suppliers and require local after-sales service.
cases.aiDraft: AI flags high channel supplier power, high entry barriers, and substitution risk from local brands.
cases.approvedUse: Accepted forces feed implications: without a partner, revenue may be bought at the expense of margin and control.
cases.outcome: The output is a test model: distribution partner, limited region, clear margin gates, and a 90-day scale/stop decision.

goal.positioningHeadline: Growth Paths is not a list of growth ideas. It is a path-selection tool: what to scale, what to test, where to enter, and what not to do now.
goal.positioningBody: AI uses organization context, interview notes, and market signals to propose options across the four Ansoff fields. The user accepts or rejects cards, and only approved options feed comparison, moves, outputs, and initiatives.

steps.title: Mission
steps.text: Growth ambition, scope, success signal, and constraints

steps.title: Input
steps.text: Signals from interviews, market, customers, and organization context

steps.title: Options
steps.text: Ansoff options: core, market, product, and diversification

steps.title: Insights
steps.text: Trade-off comparison and recommended move sequence

steps.title: Outputs
steps.text: Final source summary, output candidates, and initiative drafts

blocks.title: Option matrix
blocks.text: Growth options with impact, effort, risk, evidence, and confidence.

blocks.title: Strategic comparison
blocks.text: Trade-offs between scaling core, entering markets, product development, and diversification.

blocks.title: Recommended moves
blocks.text: A sequence: what to do now, what to test, what to defer.

blocks.title: Output candidates
blocks.text: Material for an initiative, report, deck, or follow-on exploration.

example.intro: A premium company wants to grow without margin erosion. Growth Paths compares scaling the current segment, entering a new geography, building a new product, and diversification, then sequences the moves.

cases.title: Premium company seeking growth without margin erosion
cases.context: The core segment is profitable, but growth is slowing.
cases.question: Should it scale the current market, enter a new geography, or build a new product?
evidence: Sales data shows stable margin in the current segment but a declining number of new leads.
Interviews surface demand from adjacent segments, but offer and channel fit are still unclear.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes options across all four fields: deeper core penetration, a geography test, a lighter product version, and cautious diversification.
cases.approvedUse: The user approves options with a clear first step and rejects ideas that are just wishful expansion.
cases.outcome: The sequence becomes: grow share in core, test one adjacent segment in parallel, and only then commit to a bigger bet.

cases.title: SaaS after current ICP saturation
cases.context: Retention is strong, but pipeline in the current segment is weakening.
cases.question: Should growth come from a new segment, product add-ons, or pricing?
evidence: Retention and expansion revenue are healthy, but new-logo win rate has declined for three quarters.
Customer feedback shows demand for reporting features, while sales hears requests from larger companies.
cases.aiDraft: AI creates options around core pricing packaging, mid-market entry, an analytics module, and a riskier enterprise platform move.
cases.approvedUse: Approved cards move into impact/effort/risk comparison, and AI identifies what must be validated before roadmap commitment.
cases.outcome: The recommendation is to test a new pricing package and analytics module with current customers before an expensive enterprise move.

cases.title: Services firm with strong client relationships
cases.context: Clients ask for adjacent services, but the team fears diluting specialization.
cases.question: Should it develop new offers for current clients or protect focus?
evidence: Top clients request complementary services, but project profitability drops when scope becomes too broad.
The team reports expert overload and no repeatable delivery standard for new service lines.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes product-development options for current clients, selective key-account penetration, and rejects broad diversification without proof.
cases.approvedUse: Only options with a clear ICP, delivery scope, and first commercial experiment are accepted.
cases.outcome: The plan is to create one productized service for current clients, test pricing, and then decide whether to add more offers.

goal.positioningBody: Portfolio Priority helps decide which products, initiatives, or bets to fund, maintain, test, harvest, or stop. AI proposes the first draft from context and interview evidence, but decisions flow through user approval.

process.missionText: Portfolio scope, constraints, and success signal.
process.evidenceText: Interview, market, financial, and resource signals.
process.outputsText: Trade-offs, moves, initiatives, and final summary.

outcomes.moves: Recommended moves: invest, maintain, test, harvest, stop

example.intro: A company has several products and initiatives, but budget only supports a subset. Portfolio Priority organizes the BCG cards, exposes opportunity cost, and builds the recommended action portfolio.

cases.title: Investment budget for only 3 of 9 initiatives
cases.context: The project list is long and sponsors push their own priorities.
cases.question: Which initiatives should be funded, maintained, tested, or stopped?
evidence: Each initiative has a different sponsor, but only some have evidence of growth or margin impact.
PMO data shows team overload and no clear stop/continue criteria.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes portfolio cards with growth/share/investment scores, rationale, and an invest/maintain/test/harvest/stop recommendation.
cases.approvedUse: The user approves scoring only where evidence fits, then AI builds resource trade-offs.
cases.outcome: The portfolio decision funds three initiatives, tests two with gates, and stops or defers the rest.

cases.title: Product portfolio after rapid growth
cases.context: Some products have volume but low margin; others are small but promising.
cases.question: Where should product and sales resources move?
evidence: Sales reports show high-volume low-margin products and smaller products with faster growth.
Sales interviews show the team sells what is easiest, not always what is strategic.
cases.aiDraft: AI classifies products as stars, cash cows, question marks, and dogs, then proposes sales-focus shifts.
cases.approvedUse: Approved cards expose the opportunity cost of keeping the portfolio too broad.
cases.outcome: The recommendation maintains the cash cow, funds one question mark, harvests low-margin volume, and stops products without strategic role.

cases.title: Transformation overloaded with projects
cases.context: PMO runs many parallel streams and loses delivery capacity.
cases.question: Which work is strategic and which only consumes throughput?
evidence: Project statuses look green on paper, but dependencies block key milestones.
Leader interviews show the same people are critical to several initiatives at once.
cases.aiDraft: AI scores initiatives by strategic potential, position, investment level, and real organizational capacity.
cases.approvedUse: Approved cards feed synthesis: what to fund, minimally maintain, stop, or convert into a short test.
cases.outcome: The result is a PMO relief plan: fewer active streams, restart criteria, and a list of topics to close.

goal.positioningBody: Risk & Uncertainty helps test which assumptions may fail, which risks are critical, and which resilience moves need to happen before the decision.

process.missionText: Decision, uncertainty scope, and success signal.
process.evidenceText: Interview, market, data, and operational signals.
process.riskMapText: Assumptions, risks, and scenarios as AI cards.
process.outputsText: Resilience moves, output candidates, and initiatives.

outcomes.map: Approved assumption, risk, and scenario map
outcomes.moves: Moves: validate, mitigate, monitor, hedge, escalate

example.intro: A company plans a transformation, but costs, adoption, and technology dependencies are uncertain. Risk & Uncertainty structures assumptions, risks, and scenarios, then recommends validation and mitigation moves.

cases.title: Transformation with uncertain user adoption
cases.context: The plan assumes fast rollout, but operating teams have uneven readiness.
cases.question: Which assumptions must be validated before budget commitment?
evidence: Interviews show executive enthusiasm, but line-manager skepticism and limited training capacity.
Previous rollouts were delayed not by technology, but by lack of business ownership after go-live.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes validation assumptions, adoption risks, a delay scenario, and validate/monitor/mitigate moves.
cases.approvedUse: The user accepts cards with real warning indicators such as training attendance, user activity, and workaround volume.
cases.outcome: The resilience plan includes an adoption pilot, line sponsors, early warnings, and escalation thresholds before full rollout.

cases.title: Expansion under volatile demand
cases.context: Demand is growing, but market data is mixed and dependent on a few customers.
cases.question: Which base, downside, and stress scenarios should steer the decision?
evidence: Sales sees large requests from a few customers, but pipeline is concentrated and not yet repeatable.
Market data shows category growth, but also seasonality and dependence on client investment budgets.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes base/downside/stress scenarios, demand-concentration risks, and signals to monitor before scale.
cases.approvedUse: After scenario approval, the tool builds hedge and monitor moves and suggests thresholds that pause the decision.
cases.outcome: The expansion decision gets conditions: minimum independent customers, margin gate, and early warning for conversion decline.

cases.title: Cost program under time pressure
cases.context: Leadership expects quick savings, but quality impact risk is high.
cases.question: How can the company avoid cutting critical capabilities?
evidence: Finance sees fast savings potential, but operations points to dependencies between cost and SLA.
History of similar cuts shows complaints and rework costs rising several months later.
cases.aiDraft: AI proposes quality risks, a cost rebound scenario, assumptions to validate, and mitigate/escalate moves.
cases.approvedUse: Only mitigations with an owner, trigger, and clear escalation threshold are accepted.
cases.outcome: The cost program gets guardrails: what not to cut, what to test through a pilot, and when to stop reductions.
